questions.text:
Box-and-whisker plots compare the price of two brands of running shoes from an NZ sports retailer website.

Brand A: Min $30, LQ $60, Median $90, Mean $108, UQ $130, Max $450, n = 80
Brand B: Min $70, LQ $140, Median $185, Mean $205, UQ $240, Max $600, n = 95

What percentage of Brand B running shoes cost more than $400?
questions.markingGuide: From the data, 5 out of 95 Brand B running shoes cost more than $400. 5 ÷ 95 = 0.0526 = 5.26%. Award Achieved for correct percentage with working shown.

questions.text: Compare the distributions of the price of Brand A and Brand B running shoes. Discuss similarities and differences considering centre, shift, shape, and spread. Provide numerical evidence. What conclusion can you make about which brand is more expensive?
questions.expectedAnswer: Brand B is more expensive — median $175 vs Brand A $85
questions.markingGuide: Centre: Brand B median ($175) much higher than Brand A ($85). Shift: Brand A UQ ($120) < Brand B LQ ($130), meaning no overlap in IQR. Spread: Brand B has larger range ($590 vs $455) and IQR ($100 vs $65). Shape: Both right-skewed (mean > median). Conclusion: No IQR overlap strongly supports Brand B being more expensive. Achieved = one feature. Merit = two features. Excellence = comprehensive comparison.

questions.text: Give at least one justified reason why the headphone price data may not be reliable for comparing the two brands.
questions.expectedAnswer: Data from only one website, may not represent all retailers
questions.markingGuide: Valid reasons: Data from only one website. Unknown whether prices are sale or RRP. Sample sizes differ (80 vs 95). Only NZ prices — doesn't represent other countries. Award Achieved for one justified reason.

questions.text:
A time series graph shows quarterly NZ spending on sportswear from 2012 to 2024. Spending ranges from about $400M to $900M, with a general upward trend and seasonal peaks in Q4 (Christmas).

What trends, repeating patterns, and unusual features do you notice? Support with evidence. Give at least two reasons.
questions.expectedAnswer: Increasing trend ($500M to $750M), seasonal peaks in Q4 (Christmas)
questions.markingGuide: Trend: Long-term upward from ~$500M (2012) to ~$750M (2024). Repeating: Q4 peaks (Christmas). Unusual: COVID dip in 2020, supply chain spike in 2021. Achieved = one feature. Merit = two features with evidence.

questions.text: Using the time series data on NZ sportswear spending (2012-2024), make a prediction about future spending. Explain your prediction and discuss how confident you are.
questions.expectedAnswer: Spending will continue to rise, following long-term upward trend
questions.markingGuide: Prediction: Likely to continue increasing. Seasonal Q4 peaks will persist. Confidence: Reasonable for 1-2 years as trend is established. Less confident long-term due to economic changes, technology shifts. Achieved = prediction with basic reasoning. Merit = prediction with justified confidence discussion.

questions.text:
A scatter plot shows price ($) vs cushioning level (1-10) for 90 pairs of running shoes. There is a positive trend — larger pair of shoess tend to cost more. There appear to be two clusters: level 3-5 (budget) and level 7-10 (premium).

Describe and interpret TWO different features of the relationship.
questions.expectedAnswer: Positive trend — bigger pair of shoess cost more. Two clusters: budget (32-43") and premium (50-75")
questions.markingGuide: Features: Positive relationship (larger = more expensive). Two apparent clusters (budget vs premium). Wide price variation at each size. Award Achieved for two features.

questions.text: Tama wants a 55-inch pair of shoes. Using the scatter plot with trend line, what price should he expect? How confident can you be in this prediction?
questions.expectedAnswer: About $1200 from trend line. Moderate confidence — reasonable spread at 55 inches
questions.markingGuide: Reading from trend line: approximately $1200 for 55 inches. Confidence: Moderate — 55" is in the premium cluster with reasonable data density, but there's still spread ($800-$1800 range). Achieved = reasonable price reading. Merit = price AND justified confidence.

questions.text:
Three retailers sell the same pair of shoes model:

SportZone: $950 (excl. GST), delivery $15, offers: free delivery over $1200 incl GST, 10% off if buying 2+.
pair of shoes World: $1150 (incl. GST), delivery $8, offers: 'No GST' deal (divide by 1.15), loyalty card gives 5% off.
Factory Outlet: $820 (excl. GST), delivery free if collecting from warehouse, otherwise $25.

GST rate is 15%. Ricky wants one pair of shoes. Which retailer should he choose? Show all calculations.
questions.expectedAnswer: Factory Outlet collecting: $943. pair of shoes World with loyalty: $1196.75. Mega: $1257.
questions.markingGuide: Mega: $1080 × 1.15 = $1242 + $15 delivery = $1257 (over $1200 but delivery included? No — $1242 > $1200 so free delivery). Total = $1242. pair of shoes World: $1250 / 1.15 = $1086.96 (no GST deal) + $8 = $1094.96. Or with loyalty: $1250 × 0.95 + $8 = $1195.50. Factory Outlet: $950 × 1.15 = $943 (collecting). Or + $25 = $1117.50. Best = Factory Outlet collecting at $943. Achieved = one correct calc. Excellence = comprehensive comparison.

questions.text: Ricky's current pair of shoes is level 5 but he wants to upgrade. Larger pair of shoess cost more (from the scatter plot data). Using available data, recommend the best purchasing option for Ricky.
questions.expectedAnswer: Consider Factory Outlet for best base price, but factor in travel costs to warehouse
questions.markingGuide: Key points: Larger pair of shoess cost more (scatter plot). Factory Outlet has lowest base price but requires collection. If Ricky lives far from warehouse, delivery cost matters. Buying from pair of shoes World with loyalty card may be better if he already has one. Achieved = one relevant point. Merit = points from multiple sources.

questions.text:
A survey of 2400 NZ adults asked about their exercise habits. 48% said they exercise at least 3 times per week.

Approximately how many of the 2400 respondents exercise at least 3 times per week?

Survey results on preferred exercise type: Running 24%, Gym 21%, Swimming 18%, Team sports 16%, Walking 12%, Other 9%.

Which exercise is the most preferred? Discuss how confident you would be in concluding this is genuinely the most popular.
questions.expectedAnswer: Running 24%, but Gym (21%) and Swimming (18%) close — not highly confident
questions.markingGuide: Running is most preferred at 24%. However, Gym (21%) is very close. Range across top three is only 6 percentage points. Large sample (2400) helps but small differences mean a different sample could change rankings. Achieved = identifies Running. Merit = discusses confidence.

questions.text:
Exercise preference by age group:
Under 25: Running most popular
25–35: Running and Gym tied
36–45: Gym most popular
46–55: Swimming most popular
56+: Walking most popular

Discuss two similarities or differences by age. Suggest what exercise Mia (age 34) might prefer.
questions.expectedAnswer: Younger prefer running, older prefer lower-impact. Mia likely running or gym.
questions.markingGuide: Differences: Younger people prefer running, older prefer lower-impact activities (swimming, walking). In the 25-35 bracket, running and gym are tied. For Mia (34): in the 25-35 bracket, either running or gym. Achieved = one comparison. Merit = two comparisons AND recommendation.

questions.text: James is 50, exercises 4 times per week, mostly swimming. Using survey data (by age group and frequency), recommend an exercise type and estimate how much he might spend on it monthly. Include evidence from at least two data sections.
questions.expectedAnswer: Swimming — most popular for 46-55 age group. Budget $80-$120/month based on pool pass data.
questions.markingGuide: James is 46-55 where swimming is most popular. He already swims 4× per week. Survey shows 52% of exercisers spend $50-$150/month. Recommendation: Continue swimming, budget $80-$120/month for pool membership. Achieved = recommendation with one piece of evidence. Excellence = comprehensive with cost estimate.

questions.text: How confident would you be using information from this survey to make recommendations about exercise habits?
questions.expectedAnswer: Moderately confident — large sample (2400) but may not represent all NZ adults
questions.markingGuide: Strengths: Large sample (2400). Detailed breakdowns by age and frequency. Weaknesses: Unknown how respondents were selected. Self-reported data (people may overestimate exercise). May not include all demographics equally. Achieved = one strength or weakness. Merit = both discussed.
